frozen_original.title: 11 Documented Epstein Flights: Trump Flew Palm Beach–New York on Epstein Aircraft 11 Times
frozen_original.synopsis: Flight logs document Donald Trump flying on Epstein aircraft 11 times between April 1993 and July 1998 across multiple aircraft types including a Hawker HS-125, Gulfstream II, Boeing 727, and Cessna 421. Routes were exclusively the Palm Beach–Teterboro/Newark corridor. Co-passengers included Ghislaine Maxwell on 7 of the 11 flights, alongside Mark Epstein, Eva and Celina Dubin, and unidentified women listed as 'Erin Nance Hill' and 'Sophie Biddle' in the logs. The frequency and consistency of flights — nearly 2 per year across 5 years — establish a long-standing pattern of travel intimacy between Trump and Epstein, directly contradicting Trump's claim to barely know him.

primary.title: Unverified claim of 11 Trump flights on Epstein aircraft, 1993–1998
primary.description_short: Internal draft alleges 11 Trump flights on Epstein aircraft between 1993 and 1998; the count and details remain unverified.
primary.description_medium: An internal draft alleges 11 Trump flights on Epstein aircraft from Palm Beach to the New York area between 1993 and 1998, including seven with Ghislaine Maxwell. The supplied packet lacks the flight logs and a verifiable report for that count, date span, routes, or passengers. Its prior note paraphrases a Reuters account of a DOJ-released email reporting at least eight flights from 1993–96, but provides no link or excerpt. Treat every number and association as unverified.
primary.description_long: An internal draft alleges that Donald Trump made 11 trips on Jeffrey Epstein's aircraft between April 1993 and July 1998, mainly between Palm Beach and the New York area. It says Ghislaine Maxwell was on seven of the flights and lists Mark Epstein, Eva and Celina Dubin, and two other named passengers. Those details are retained only as supplied claims: the packet does not include the flight logs or an opened source that establishes the count, dates, routes, aircraft, or passenger identities. The prior hold note paraphrases Reuters as describing a DOJ-released prosecutor email about at least eight flights from 1993 to 1996, including at least four with Maxwell, but it provides neither the article URL nor a literal excerpt; that note does not verify this record. The alleged travel, even if documented, would not by itself establish knowledge of Epstein's crimes or misconduct by any passenger. Keep the record internal until the logs or a verifiable contemporaneous report can support a narrower account.

frozen_original.title: Trump Holds Up Blank Paper Claiming It's His Healthcare Plan
frozen_original.synopsis: At a campaign rally, Trump held up what appeared to be a blank or nearly blank piece of paper, presenting it as his healthcare plan. After years of promising to replace the Affordable Care Act with a better plan, Trump had no substantive healthcare proposal to show. The image of a president holding up a blank page as his healthcare policy became a widely shared symbol of the lack of substance behind his policy rhetoric. Healthcare policy experts and journalists who examined Trump's actual healthcare proposals noted they contained no specific mechanisms for covering preexisting conditions or reducing costs. The moment crystallized years of criticism that Trump's healthcare promises were entirely performative.

primary.title: Trump Promised Better Health Care but Offered No Specific Plan at Town Hall
primary.description_short: At an October 15, 2020 town hall, Trump promised better, cheaper health care but offered no specific plan details.
primary.description_medium: At a town hall on October 15, 2020, Trump was asked about plans to lower health-care costs. The Boston Globe reported that he promised “much better health care under a much better price” but had yet to outline a specific plan. This supports a narrow description of that exchange; it does not document a blank-paper display.
primary.description_long: On October 15, 2020, Donald Trump took questions at a town hall and was asked about his plans to lower health-care costs. The Boston Globe reported that he attacked the Affordable Care Act, promised “much better health care under a much better price,” and had yet to outline a specific plan. This supports a narrow description of the exchange and a promise, not an enacted program. The frozen synopsis’s scene of Trump holding a blank sheet at an October 15 rally is not supported by this contemporaneous account, which describes a town hall and no paper prop. Searches also surfaced later October reporting about a separate 60 Minutes interview and a healthcare-accomplishments binder; that later story does not establish the alleged October 15 rally scene and is not substituted here. This card preserves only the documented October 15 health-policy answer. The available report gives no coverage mechanism, cost estimate, bill, or subsequent outcome. It also does not establish whether Trump had a separate proposal elsewhere; the description is limited to his answer at this event.

frozen_original.title: Trump Ends All Federal Support for Contraceptive Access
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, the Trump administration eliminated federal programs and funding streams specifically supporting contraceptive access, including grants for contraceptive counseling, over-the-counter contraception access initiatives, and emergency contraception stocking requirements. The administration rescinded the Affordable Care Act contraceptive mandate guidance that had required employer health insurance plans to cover contraception without cost-sharing, enabling a broad exemption for any employer citing moral or religious objections. Public health organizations estimated that millions of women would lose free contraceptive coverage under employer-sponsored health plans. The rollbacks occurred simultaneously with the defunding of Title X and elimination of Planned Parenthood Medicaid participation, creating a compounding elimination of reproductive healthcare access for low-income women.

primary.disposition: Replaced the unsupported claim of an all-program February rollback with a documented, narrower action: temporary withholding notices for 22 Title X grants issued March 31, effective April 1, 2025. The broader ACA-repeal and all-support claims remain unverified.
primary.title: Administration Temporarily Withholds 22 Title X Grants
primary.description_short: On March 31, 2025, Title X grantees were notified that the administration would temporarily withhold funding for 22 grants beginning April 1.
primary.description_medium: On March 31, 2025, 16 Title X grantees received notices that the Trump administration was temporarily withholding funds for 22 fiscal year 2025 grants, effective April 1. Title X supports family-planning care, including contraception. The Guttmacher Institute estimated that if the withholding became permanent, at least 834,000 people could lose access to Title X-funded care over a year; that figure is conditional, not a count of confirmed losses.
primary.description_long: On March 31, 2025, 16 Title X grantees received notices that the Trump administration was temporarily withholding funding from 22 fiscal year 2025 grants, effective April 1. Title X supports family-planning services, including contraception, for low-income people. The Guttmacher Institute reported that all 13 direct grants to Planned Parenthood affiliates were included among the 22. It estimated that, if the withholding became permanent, at least 834,000 people could lose access to Title X-funded care in a year. That estimate is conditional: it is not a count of people already deprived of care. The evidence supports a temporary, targeted withholding in April 2025. This card does not repeat the original assertions that all federal contraceptive support ended in February or that the Affordable Care Act’s contraceptive coverage requirement was rescinded then; the cited record establishes the Title X grant action. The estimate and consequences remain attributed to Guttmacher, and the sources reviewed do not establish whether the withheld funds were later restored or how many patients lost services.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

impact_proposal.confidence_reason: The notices and temporary funding action are documented; the largest cited access effect is a conditional estimate if withholding became permanent.
impact_proposal.rationale: The administration temporarily withheld funding for a portion of Title X grants, a program that supports family planning and contraception. The potential access loss is serious but remains conditional, so the estimate is not counted as realized harm; no evidence here establishes institutional damage, procedural abuse, or private gain.
impact_proposal.basis: Sixteen grantees were notified of temporary withholding for 22 FY2025 grants effective April 1; Guttmacher estimated potential effects if the withholding became permanent.
